results.abstract_text:
PROJECT SUMMARY/ABSTRACT
 Most therapies that target microbiome composition do not have a detectable impact on the gut microbiome
and are not robust to the interpersonal diversity and plasticity of the community in human hosts. To develop a
better mechanistic understanding of the microbe-host relationship and more effective microbiome-mediated
therapies, approaches based on functional modulation of the gut microbiome are necessary. However, these
approaches have been difficult to develop. Attaining long-term engraftment in the luminal environment has
proven to be quite difficult, and even once engraftment has been achieved, a change in physiology or
improvement of pathologic phenotype has not yet been demonstrated. There is a critical need for a tool that will
allow investigators to “knock-in” functions into the gut microbiome and investigate their effects on the luminal
milieu and, ultimately, physiology in conventionally-raised hosts in non-sterile conditions. The investigators
propose a novel approach to address this need by using native bacteria as chassis for the introduction of specific
functions into the luminal environment. The proposal's innovation is a new strategy that allows the quick and
effective “knock-in” of a beneficial function in a sustained manner into conventional hosts. To date they have
demonstrated that tractable native bacteria can be engineered to express a beneficial function ex vivo,
reintroduced to the host, engraft the entire gut of the host, and deliver an intended beneficial function. These
functions can affect host physiology, help determine the effect of specific bacterial functions and potentially
alleviate disease. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that long-term colonization and functional change in
the gut microbiome of a conventional host can be performed effectively with engineered native bacteria.
 In the next five years, the investigators will continue the development of this technology and better
understand the chassis-host interactions that will aid in the development of live bacterial therapeutics for clinical
use. First, the investigators will engineer regulatory systems for the transgene of interest, including a sense and
control, protein secretion, and biocontainment circuit. They will test whether these systems function in vivo in
hosts that are in a non-sterile environment. In addition, they will assess the natural biocontainment of engineered
native bacteria among co-housed hosts. Second, they will determine how the niche for a bacterial chassis affects
function delivery and whether multiple functions can be delivered by the same chassis or whether different
chassis are necessary for the delivery of multiple functions. Finally, the investigators will determine the role of
microbial community in amplifying the effects of a transgene of interest in gnotobiotic mice. The expected
outcome of the proposed studies is attainment of fundamental biological knowledge of how the gut microbiome
can be functionally manipulated. These studies will have a positive translational impact because they will
demonstrate that synthetic biology approaches can lead to the development of curative interventions to some of
the most debilitating and costly chronic diseases.

results.abstract_text: (a)Engineering a phage to have multiple tails broadening its host range. The ability of a phage to infect particular species and strains of bacteria is determined by the ability of its tail fiber protein to use as the specific receptors for phage binding some of the proteins exposed on the bacterial surface. Mutations in these proteins make bacteria resistant to the phage. Our approach is based on developing a E. coli based technology to easily fuse to or substitute the tail of T7 phage with one or more tails from K. pneumoniae specific phages to enable the derivative phage to infect several strains of KPC+ K. pneumonae. T7 based platform has a number of practical advantages for fighting KPC+ K. pneumonia infections. Producing large numbers of K. pneumoniae specific phages in the nonpathogenic E. coli is profoundly cost effective. Having one phage capable of destroying several K. pneumoniae strains in not only cost effective as well, but it will eliminate phage exclusion, which is a potential complication of using several separate phage strains simultaneously in order to expand the host spectrum. Eventually, our system could also allow us to overcome developing phage resistance by producing a multitude of mutant phage tails. In order to understand the nature of phage resistance and to recover the sequences of "active" tails, we have investigated the prevalence, types and characteristics of K. pneumonae phages in hospitalized patients. To express the K. pneumoniae phage tails in the bacteriophage T7, we have utilized recombineering system based on Red recombinase functions from the bacteriophage lambda introduced in E. coli . Selection is based on using T7 mutants that contain stop codons in tail fiber genes and are therefore incapable of infecting bacteria; upon recombination with synthetically produced PCR product that corrects these stop codons and simultaneously introduces a foreign tail, the phage can infect and propagate in E. coli. This is the first time that this rapid and versatile system has been used to make changes to T7 genome. A manuscript describing the procedure has been submitted. (b) Construction of Klebsiella phage that plates on E. coli and vice versa. Our long term goal is to develop a single-chassis platform phage that is amenable to broaden its host range. Our selected target host was the clinical KPC isolate. In the past, modification of a host receptor binding proteins (RBPs) present in the phage tail complex have been implied in broadening the host range of handful of phages with narrow margin of success rate. WE genetically modified a Klebsiella ST258 phage, called Pharr. We successfully engineered the Pharr phage with an E. coli phage T7 tail by adding the T7 RBP gene in to the Pharr genome, and demonstrated the ability of the new phage to grow and form plaques on E. coli host. However, when we similarly engineered the E. coli phage T7 with RBP from the Klebsiella phage Pharr, the resultant phage was only capable of infecting and killing the targeted KPC hst without yielding progeny virions. Such limitation in widening the host range to its full potential by modifying the RBPs hinges on the spectrum of strategies that bacteria uses to protect themselves from phage infection. Common strategies include phage adsorption inhibition, blocking DNA entry, restriction-modification systems, toxin-antitoxin systems, and CRISPR-Cas systems, all of which were largely derived from the phage-host interaction studies of few model systems. Whether any of these or some undiscovered system is active while targeting a novel host requires a system-level understanding of phage-host interaction at the genome-wide scale. To address this, we generated a plasmid library of K. pneumonia genome into E. coli host and looked for a phage growth inhibition factor that causes growth inhibition of T7 phage in E. coli host. We identified such clones and studied one of them further. We were also able to isolate a phage suppressor mutation of T7. This suggests that evolution of T7 against other unknow restriction factors imposed by Klebsiella genome is possible. We are currently performing a serial passage experiment to evolve T7 phage to an extent where it can grow in the K. pneumonia host. We anticipate a successfully evolved T7 phage to accumulate multiple changes in its genome reflecting the molecular interplay between T7 and Klebsiella genome. Furthermore, this strategy will be adopted to target host of different genera such as Yersinia, Acenitobacter, Pseudomonas, and Salmonella, establishing an effective way of engineering phages in general. (c) Engineering T7 phage to express antimicrobial peptide to address the phage resistance issue: Trojan Horse. In the current situation of this antibiotic crisis, bacteriophages are being explored as an antibacterial treatment option for several reasons; phages specifically lyse target bacteria without causing any disruption to the normal flora, phage application is not known to cause toxicity, and the production of phages is relatively simple, less time consuming, and cost effective. Bacteria on the other hand are also known to evolve with complex phage resistance mechanism, limiting the clinical use of phages. To overcome such limitation, natural phages can be genetically engineered to equip with extra pay-load that can potentially minimize the emergence of resistance. Because cationic antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are known to have broad-spectrum killing effect on most gram-negative bacteria, expression of AMPs from the phage genome is hypothesized to cover both the sensitive and resistance bacteria during its utilization. To test this idea, a select group of commercially synthetized AMPs were first tested in-vitro and found to be ineffective in killing the T7 host E. coli, but their application on the T7 resistant bacterial lawn showed robust killing activity. Interestingly, bacteria that emerged as resistant to these peptides were found to become sensitive to T7 again, suggesting combination of phage and AMPs would restrict the escape of bacteria by resistance mechanism. We have recently performed the whole genome sequencing of phage and AMP sensitive and resistant hosts derived from a single lineage. Sequence comparison will allow us to understand if the relation between AMP resistance host that become susceptible to phage can be linked to a conserved phenomenon. Our preliminary result indicates that genes in the Lps and Cps biosynthesis pathway are primarily affected by phage and AMPs action. In parallel we are engineering T7 phage either to express or surface display AMPs during its lytic growth cycle. Such engineered phages will be tested for their effectiveness in lowering the resistance problem. Using the above protocols we constructed phage that carry a new tail imparting the ability to plate on the corresponding new host.
